To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

individual cognitive maps tend not to recognize trade-offs, but the collective map that resulted after aggregating all individual maps did recognize trade-offs, and that lags in individual maps reduced the likelihood of recognizing trade-offs.

individual cognitive maps of wildfire risk in the Eastern Cascadian ecoregion of Oregon are characterized by a strong bias against perception of tradeoffs, and that this bias decreases with the heterogeneity of the causal factors that mediate the relationship between action and valued outcomes.

the perception of trade-offs by individuals is less likely when there are more factors that mediate the effect of an intervention on multiple valued outcomes, but that the likelihood of perceiving trade-offs increases when the factors that mediate an effect on multiple valued outcomes are more diverse.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people perceive and respond to trade-offs in a social-ecological context that is characterized by complexity.

the cognitive processes through which individuals perceive trade-offs in complex social-ecological settings and with the implications of this for the collective perception of trade-off among individuals.

the cognitive and collective processes through which people make sense of complex social-ecological dynamics, and how these processes influence their ability to identify trade-offs in the face of environmental challenges such as wildfire risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results presented in this article provide a basis for further research on cognitive mapping and trade-offs in social-ecological settings, but that the results themselves do not support the conclusion that cognitive maps can be used as a tool to identify trade-offs in social ecological systems.

the complexity of the social and ecological systems in central Oregon and other wildfire-prone regions of the American West and the world, is not only a challenge but also an opportunity for understanding how to mitigate wildfire risk and other complex environmental challenges through the development of new approaches and strategies.

this paper is a good example of how to use cognitive mapping to explore the perception of complexity and tradeoffs in wildfire management, but it does not really provide any new information on how these perceptions are formed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found that the complexity of social and ecological systems, in particular, can be a barrier to the perception of trade-offs by individuals, but that it can also be an enabler of collective perception of tradeoffs.
the complexity of wildfire management in a social-ecological setting can be addressed by understanding the cognitive maps of stakeholders and how those maps are affected by features of complexity.
the complexity of a system is a key factor to consider when evaluating how people perceive trade-offs and make choices.
The main takeaway from our work is that

complexity can both facilitate and constrain perception of trade-offs and that the effects of complexity on perception of trade-offs vary depending on whether one is examining the cognitive maps of individuals or the collective.
the cognitive complexity of individuals and groups is a critical factor for effective wildfire risk mitigation, and that it can be assessed through the study of cognitive maps.

, although complexity may limit individual perception of trade-offs and the ability to act accordingly, it also increases the likelihood of collective perception of tradeoffs, thus opening the door to effective collective action.
